story.e:
On the very same Sunday that Jesus rose, two disciples were walking from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus. They were sad. As they walked, they talked and argued about everything that had happened over the past few days.

Then Jesus Himself came up and walked along with them. But they did not recognize Him, because something kept their eyes from seeing who He was. Jesus asked them what they were talking about. They stopped, looking sad, and told Him that the man they believed to be a great prophet had been crucified. *But we were hoping that He was the One who would redeem Israel*, they said. To redeem means to set the people free. We were hoping: that is in the past. Their hope had been broken.

Jesus answered, *O foolish ones!* Then, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them everything that was written about Himself in the Scriptures, which means the Bible. It was a long walk, and a long conversation.

When they reached the village, evening was coming. They begged Him to stay with them. Jesus sat down with them at the table. He took the bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized Him! But at that very moment He disappeared from their sight. They said to each other, *Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road?* Their eyes were opened at a shared table.

Thomas, one of the twelve disciples, was not there when Jesus first appeared to the disciples and showed them His hands and His side. When the others told him, Thomas answered, *Unless I see the nail marks in His hands and put my finger where the nails have been, I will never believe.* He wanted to see and touch the wounds. In other words, he asked for the same thing the others had already been given.

A week later Jesus came again and spoke to Thomas: *Put your finger here and look at My hands.* Then Thomas said, *My Lord and my God!* Jesus answered, *Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.* Those words are about us too, the people who read this story today.

Jesus appeared to His disciples many more times. Once He told them, *You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.* A witness is someone who tells what they have seen and heard. So the good news does not stay in one place; it travels far.

Then Jesus led them out as far as Bethany, a village near Jerusalem. He lifted up His hands and blessed His disciples. He was taken up into heaven before their very eyes, and a cloud hid Him from their sight. The disciples just stood there, staring at the sky. Then two men dressed in white stood beside them and said, *Men of Galilee, why do you stand here looking into the sky?* Their job was not to stand and wait, but to go and be witnesses.
story.m:
On Easter day two disciples were heading from Jerusalem toward the village of Emmaus, which Luke says was sixty stadia, roughly eleven kilometers, from the city. On the way they talked and argued about everything that had happened. Then Jesus Himself came up and walked with them. He stepped right into the middle of their questions. But their eyes were kept from recognizing Him. What kept them, the text does not tell us. Jesus asked what they were discussing, and they stood still, looking sad, and then spoke the most painful sentence of all: *But we were hoping that He was the One who would redeem Israel.* They said it in the past tense: their hope was broken.

Jesus replied, *O foolish ones, how slow are your hearts to believe all that the prophets have spoken!* Then, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself. Foolish ones is a strong word, but Jesus does not walk away; He walks the whole road with them. Love and honesty can go together.

By evening they reached the village and urged Him to stay with them. Jesus sat down at the table with them, took the bread, spoke a blessing, broke it, and gave it to them. Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Him, and He disappeared from their sight. They said to each other, *Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road?* They had felt it along the way, but only afterward did they understand what they had felt. It is all right if something only comes together later: that is how it was for the disciples too.

John's Gospel tells about Thomas. He was not there when Jesus first appeared to the disciples and showed them His hands and His side. Thomas said that unless he saw the nail marks in His hands, he would never believe. A week later Jesus appeared and gave him what he had asked for: *Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe.* Jesus did not scold him for asking: there is no shame in asking for evidence. Thomas answered, *My Lord and my God!* It was the questioner who reached the clearest confession. Jesus added, *Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.* Those words speak to every later reader.

The book of Acts, also written by Luke, says that Jesus appeared to the disciples over a period of forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God. So these meetings were not one-off events. According to Luke's Gospel, He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures and told them that repentance for the forgiveness of sins would be proclaimed in His name to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. *You are witnesses of these things.* They did not appoint themselves as witnesses; Jesus called them that. Witnesses speak about what they have seen. The starting point was Jerusalem, the very place where, only weeks before, everything had gone so wrong.

Their power would come from the Holy Spirit: *you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.* Jerusalem is the beginning, Judea and Samaria are the surrounding region, and the ends of the earth make the full circle. In Luke's Gospel Jesus blessed them near Bethany. In Acts He was taken up before their very eyes, and a cloud hid Him from their sight. Two men dressed in white said to them, *Men of Galilee, why do you stand here looking into the sky?* This same Jesus will come back in the same way they had seen Him go into heaven.

If you have ever had a hope that was broken, and it still weighs heavily on you, talk about it with an adult you trust: a parent, a teacher, a pastor.

**What the Bible does not say:** It does not tell us what kept the disciples' eyes from recognizing Jesus at Emmaus, or how He disappeared from the table. It does not say whether Thomas actually touched Jesus' wounds: it records only his confession. It does not say where heaven is, or when Jesus will return.
story.h:
This part brings together three texts: Luke 24 (Emmaus, the commission, and the farewell), John 20 (Thomas), and Acts 1 (the forty days and the ascension). Luke's Gospel and the book of Acts come from the same author; the opening lines of Acts point back to the first book (Acts 1:1). That matters, because we will soon meet a difference inside this one author's work.

**Verses 15-16.** According to Luke 24:15, Jesus joined the two disciples while they were talking and arguing: He stepped into the middle of their dispute. Verse 16 says *their eyes were kept from recognizing Him*. The Greek uses the passive voice here (literally, their eyes were being held back), and it does not give the reason. The passive hides who or what was holding them back. Many readers supply God here, others grief or the fact that they were not expecting Him, but the text says neither. The same construction returns in verse 31: *their eyes were opened*, again passive, again with no named subject. The two verses form a frame, and on both sides of it stands the same silence.

**Where was Emmaus?** We do not know for certain. Luke gives sixty stadia from Jerusalem (about 11 km), but a few manuscripts read one hundred sixty. There are several candidate sites, and none is proven. If a map shows Emmaus with confidence, that is a choice, not a fact.

**Hope in the past tense.** *But we were hoping that He was the One who would redeem Israel* (24:21). Redemption here means the freeing of the nation, and the past tense marks the collapse of that hope. In verse 25 Jesus calls them foolish ones, and in verse 27, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explains the Scriptures.

**At the table, not during the explanation.** Even the long explanation does not lead them to recognize Him. Then they sit down, Jesus takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, gives it to them, and at that moment their eyes are opened (24:30-31). Recognition happens at the table, not during the teaching. According to verse 31, Jesus vanishes from their sight at that same moment. He does not stay with them at the table after they recognize Him: now the news is theirs to carry, and that same evening they go back to Jerusalem (24:33). Verse 32 looks back: *Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?* This shows that understanding came afterward: they felt it along the way, but understood only later. John's Gospel states the same principle more than once: the disciples understood what Jesus had said and done only after the resurrection (John 2:22; 12:16).

**Thomas.** Many call him Doubting Thomas, but it is worth looking at what he actually asked. John 20:25: *Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.* According to John 20:20, Jesus had already shown the others His hands and His side. So Thomas asked for the same sign, the wounds, that the others had already received, not for something different or greater. And Jesus gave it to him (20:27): *Put your finger here and look at My hands.* In verse 29 He does not hold the request for evidence against him. What the text does not tell us is whether Thomas actually touched Him: it records the confession, not the touch. Many paintings show the touch; the text does not.

**My Lord and my God.** Thomas's confession stands in John 20:28, near the end of the book, and many regard it as the clearest confession of Jesus' divinity in the Gospels. John 1:1 began by saying that the Word was God. John 20:28 closes that frame: what the author said in his own voice at the start, a character says at the end, and not a scholar but the questioner. Verse 29, *Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed*, is not an accusation against Thomas; it is addressed to those who would never see Jesus in person.

**The commission.** According to Luke 24:47, repentance for the forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in His name to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. Verse 48: *You are witnesses of these things.* Being witnesses is Jesus' assignment, not the disciples' own decision.

**The manuscript question at 24:51.** *While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven.* The words and was carried up into heaven are missing from a few important manuscripts, including Codex Bezae. Most scholars think the original text included them, but the question is open and worth noting.

**One day or forty?** Luke 24 can be read as a single long day: the tomb in the morning, Emmaus in the afternoon, the disciples in the evening, and then apparently the farewell. Acts 1:3, however, says that Jesus appeared to them over a period of forty days and spoke about the kingdom of God: the risen Jesus went on teaching His disciples. The same author gives both, so these are not two opposing sources. The usual explanation is that the end of the Gospel compresses events and leaves the detailed timeline for the start of Acts. That is possible, even likely, but Luke 24 on its own does not point that way. This is a real tension, not an error, and it is better to name it than to smooth it over.

**Taken up, and the ancient picture of the world.** In the ancient picture of the world, heaven was above. The text speaks in the language of its time, just as we speak of the sunrise even though we know the sun does not actually rise. Taken up is not a modern astronomical claim about where heaven is. The cloud is a recurring biblical image of God's presence (Exodus 13:21; 40:34; Matthew 17:5).

**From Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.** Acts 1:8 gives the outline of the whole book: Jerusalem (chapters 1-7), Judea and Samaria (from chapter 8), and the ends of the earth (Paul's journeys as far as Rome). According to Acts 1:11, Jesus will come back in the same way they saw Him go into heaven: this is about the manner, not the time.

**What the Bible does not say:** It does not say what kept them from recognizing Jesus at Emmaus. It does not tell us for certain where Emmaus was, and even its distance varies between manuscripts. It does not say whether Thomas actually touched Jesus. It does not resolve the difference between one day and forty days: the proposed solutions are ours, not the text's. It does not say where heaven is, and it does not explain the physics of the ascension. And it does not say when Jesus will return: anyone who reads a date out of it is reading more than is there.

bio.hu: Idős pap, aki a templomban szolgált, amikor az angyal megszólította. Nem hitte el, hogy fia születhet, ezért kilenc hónapig nem tudott beszélni. Amikor végre megszólalt, nem zúgolódott: éneket mondott Isten irgalmáról. Az ő fia lett Keresztelő János.
bio.en: An elderly priest serving in the temple when the angel spoke to him. He could not believe that he would have a son, and so for nine months he could not speak. When at last he spoke, he did not complain: he sang of God's mercy. His son was John the Baptist.

hu.q: Mit tanít Zakariás története a kételkedésről?
o: A kétely nem zárja ki Isten ígéretét

en.q: What does Zechariah's story teach about doubt?
o: Doubt does not cancel God's promise
God works only with the faultless

bio.hu: Názáreti ács, aki csendben, szó nélkül cselekedett. Amikor nehéz helyzetbe került, nem akarta megszégyeníteni Máriát. Az álomban kapott szóra felkelt, és megtette, amit Isten kért — kétszer is útnak indult a család védelmében. A Bibliában egyetlen mondatát sem olvassuk: csak azt, amit tett.
bio.en: A carpenter of Nazareth who acted quietly, without words. When he found himself in a hard situation he did not want to shame Mary. At the word he received in a dream he got up and did what God asked — twice he set out to protect the family. The Bible records not one sentence he spoke: only what he did.

en.q: What was Joseph's work?
What did he not want to do to Mary?
How did God speak to him?
o: Through an angel in the temple

hu.q: Mit tett József az álom után?

en.q: What did Joseph do after the dream?
o: He got up and did what was asked

hu.q: Hová vitte a családot a második álom után?

en.q: Where did he take the family after the second dream?
To which town did they return from Egypt?

hu.q: Mi különös József szerepében a Bibliában?

en.q: What is remarkable about Joseph's part in the Bible?
o: Not one spoken word of his is recorded
A csendes, hűséges tett is beszél
Aki nem beszél, az nem fontos

en.q: What does Joseph's story teach?
o: Someone who stays silent does not matter

bio.hu: Fiatal lány Názáretben, akit az angyal köszöntött. Nem értette, hogyan lehetséges, amit hallott, és meg is kérdezte — de a végén azt mondta: történjék velem a te szavad szerint. Később éneket mondott arról, hogy Isten letaszítja a hatalmasokat, és felemeli a megalázottakat.
bio.en: A young girl in Nazareth whom the angel greeted. She did not understand how what she heard could happen, and she asked — but in the end she said: let it be with me according to your word. Later she sang that God brings down rulers and lifts up the humble.

en.q: In which town did Mary live?
Which angel greeted her?
What did Mary ask the angel?
o: What will I get for it?
Történjék velem a te szavad szerint

en.q: What did Mary finally answer?
o: Let it be with me according to your word

hu.q: Kihez ment el Mária a hír után?

en.q: Whom did Mary visit after the news?
What is Mary's song about?

hu.q: Mit tett Mária a pásztorok szavai után?

en.q: What did Mary do after the shepherds' words?
o: She treasured these things in her heart
Lehet igent mondani akkor is, ha nem értünk mindent

en.q: What does Mary's yes teach?
o: We can say yes even when we do not understand everything
God speaks only to the brave

bio.hu: Adószedő volt, akit a környezete megvetett, mert a rómaiaknak gyűjtött. Jézus elment a vámasztalához, és csak ennyit mondott: követs engem. Máté felkelt, és otthagyta a pénzt. Vacsorát adott, és odahívta a saját barátait is — azokat, akiket mások messze elkerültek.
bio.en: He was a tax collector, despised by those around him because he collected for the Romans. Jesus went to his tax booth and said only: follow me. Matthew got up and left the money behind. He gave a dinner and invited his own friends too — the very people others kept away from.

en.q: What was Matthew's work?
Why were tax collectors despised?
o: Because they collected for the Romans

en.q: Where did Jesus find Matthew?
What did Jesus say to him?
What did Matthew do?
o: He got up and left the money behind

hu.q: Kiket hívott meg Máté a vacsorára?
o: A saját barátait, akiket mások elkerültek

en.q: Whom did Matthew invite to the dinner?
o: His own friends, whom others avoided

hu.q: Mit mondtak erre azok, akik kifogásolták?

en.q: What did those who objected say?

o: Nem az egészségeseknek kell az orvos

en.q: What did Jesus answer?
o: It is not the healthy who need a doctor
Jézus olyanokat is elhív, akiket mások leírtak

en.q: What does Matthew's calling teach?
o: Jesus calls even those others have written off
Only good people may follow him

bio.hu: A pusztában élt, teveszőr ruhában, és nem kímélt senkit: a hatalmasoknak is kimondta az igazat. Mégis azt mondta magáról, hogy ő csak hang, és nem méltó megoldani Jézus sarujának szíját. Amikor a tanítványai a népszerűsége miatt aggódtak, így felelt: neki növekednie kell, nekem pedig kisebbé lennem.
bio.en: He lived in the desert in clothes of camel hair, and he spared no one: he told the truth even to the powerful. Yet he said of himself that he was only a voice, and that he was not worthy to untie the strap of Jesus' sandals. When his disciples worried about his popularity, he answered: he must become greater, I must become less.

en.q: Where did John the Baptist live?
What did he wear?

o: Térjetek meg, mert elközelített Isten országa

en.q: What did he preach?
o: Repent, for the kingdom of God has come near

en.q: Where did he baptise?
What did he call himself?
What did he say about Jesus when he saw him?

hu.q: Mit felelt, amikor a tanítványai aggódtak a népszerűsége miatt?
o: Neki növekednie kell, nekem kisebbé lennem

en.q: What did he answer when his disciples worried about his popularity?
o: He must become greater, I must become less
I will win the people back

hu.q: Kinek mondta ki az igazat, pedig veszélyes volt?

en.q: To whom did he speak the truth even though it was dangerous?

o: Nem baj, ha nem mi vagyunk a középpontban
A nehéz igazságot el kell hallgatni

en.q: What does John's story teach?
o: It is all right not to be at the centre
We must always aim to be first

bio.hu: Idős ember, aki egész életében arra várt, hogy meglássa Isten szabadítását. Amikor a templomban karjába vette a kisgyermek Jézust, azt mondta: most már elbocsáthatod szolgádat. De nem csak örömet mondott Máriának: azt is, hogy ez a gyermek sokaknak megütközés lesz, és a te szívedet is tőr járja át.
bio.en: An old man who waited all his life to see God's salvation. When he took the child Jesus in his arms in the temple he said: now you may let your servant go. But he did not speak only joy to Mary: he also said that this child would be a stumbling block to many, and that a sword would pierce her heart too.

en.q: What did Simeon wait for all his life?
Where did he meet Jesus?
What did Simeon do with the child?
o: He took him in his arms
He blessed him outside the temple

en.q: What did Simeon say?
o: Now you may let your servant go

hu.q: Mit mondott Simeon Máriának a nehéz jövőről?
o: Hogy a szívét tőr járja át

en.q: What did Simeon tell Mary about the hard future?
o: That a sword would pierce her heart

hu.q: Ki volt még ott a templomban?

en.q: Who else was there in the temple?

hu.q: Mit mondott Simeon a gyermekről a népek felé?

en.q: What did Simeon say about the child for the nations?
o: He will be a light for the nations

hu.q: Mit tanít Simeon története a várakozásról?

en.q: What does Simeon's story teach about waiting?
o: Even a long wait can be fulfilled
Only the young see good things
